content:
Yesterday we saw the rebellion of Israel at Kadesh. The people wept through the night, longed to return to Egypt, and even wished to stone Joshua and Caleb. Then the glory of Yahweh appeared before all the people. Today we continue in Numbers 14:11-20, and we come to a very solemn moment, for Yahweh now speaks about judgment, and one man stands in the gap to plead for the people.

Yahweh said to Moses, "How long will these people treat me with contempt? Will they never believe me, even after all the miraculous signs I have done among them?". Then God made a startling declaration. He said He would strike the people with a plague and destroy them, and He said to Moses, "But I will make you into a nation greater and mightier than they are!". This is an amazing statement. God offered to set aside the whole nation of Israel and to build a new nation out of Moses himself. Any ordinary man might have been tempted by such an offer. To become the father of a great nation, to have his own name magnified, to be free from a stubborn and rebellious people; this was a great personal honour placed before Moses. But Moses did not think of himself.
He thought of Yahweh's name and of Yahweh's people. Instead of accepting the offer, he began to plead for Israel.

Moses answered God with a beautiful argument. He said that the Egyptians and the surrounding nations would hear of it. He said that if Yahweh destroyed the whole nation at once, the nations would say that Yahweh was not able to bring His people into the land He had promised them, and so He had killed them in the wilderness. Moses was concerned that the name and honour of Yahweh would be spoken against among the nations. His plea was not, "Spare them because they are good." His plea was, "Act for the sake of Your own great name." Then Moses appealed to the very character of Yahweh. He said, "Please, Lord, prove that your power is as great as you have claimed" (Numbers 14:17), and he repeated the words God Himself had spoken, "Yahweh is slow to anger and filled with unfailing love, forgiving every kind of sin and rebellion" (Numbers 14:18). Moses repeated the very nature that Yahweh had revealed. And then he prayed, "In keeping with your magnificent, unfailing love, please pardon the sins of this people, just as you have forgiven them ever since they left Egypt".

And Yahweh answered, "I will pardon them as you have requested". What a wonderful thing this is. One man stood between a whole nation and destruction, and God heard his prayer. But in the same passage where God describes His mercy, He also uses words that many people find difficult, and we must look at them carefully. God said in Numbers 14:18 that He does not leave the guilty unpunished, but visits "the sins of the parents upon their children; the entire family is affected; even children in the third and fourth generations."

At first this sounds troubling. Does it mean that Yahweh punishes innocent children for the sins their parents committed? Does He hold a child guilty for a wrong that the child never did? This is a very important question, and Scripture itself gives us the clear answer, for Yahweh does not contradict Himself. In fact, in another place Yahweh states the exact opposite of what people fear these words mean; He declares plainly that the child will not carry the guilt of the parent, nor the parent the guilt of the child. So which is it? How can Yahweh say He visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, and yet also say the son shall not bear the guilt of the father? These two statements seem to stand against each other, and unless we understand what the word "visit" truly means, we may badly misunderstand the very heart of Yahweh. That is where we will continue tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We thank You that when Israel deserved judgment, You listened to the plea of one man. Teach us the heart of Moses, who thought not of his own honour but of Your great name.

Make us people who stand in the gap for others rather than seeking our own gain.

We thank You that You are slow to anger and filled with unfailing love.

Help us to trust Your character even when Your words are hard for us to understand.

"But you, O Lord, are a God of compassion and mercy, slow to anger and filled with unfailing love." - Psalm 86:15

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
